title: Al-Fajr: the soul at rest
hookLine: O soul at peace, return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing (89:27–30)

cards: A key turns in the lock after a long trip. The smell of a familiar place, the bag dropped by the door, shoulders coming down an inch nobody knew they were up. That's rest: not only stopping, but arriving.
Al-Fajr has been a hard surah. Old cities falling, the orphan neglected, then a scene of the Day itself, the earth ground to dust and people wishing they'd done more.
Then, in its last four verses, the voice changes completely. It turns to one soul and speaks to it like someone coming home. Today: the soul at rest.

teach.b: Verse twenty-one: the earth ground down, flattened. Your Lord comes, and the angels, rank on rank. And the human being remembers, too late: if only I had sent something ahead for this life of mine.
Then verse twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" Then: enter among My servants, enter My Garden.
After all the thunder, the ending is spoken gently, to one soul. The Arabic is an-nafs al-mutma'innah.
Mutma'innah means settled, at rest, reassured, the way water settles when you stop stirring it. It's the same root the Qur'an uses elsewhere: in the remembrance of God, hearts find rest.

Later scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, describe three states of the soul, drawn from three places in the Qur'an: the soul that pushes toward harm, from Surah twelve; the soul that blames itself, from Surah seventy-five; and this one, the soul at rest.
Some read them not as three kinds of people, but as three states one person can move through, sometimes in a single afternoon. Then the last phrase: raadiyatan mardiyyah.
The soul is content with its Lord, and its Lord is content with it. It runs both ways. These verses are often recalled in grief, the picture of someone loved being called home.
And the word is return. Not go somewhere strange. Go back to where you came from.

how: Muslims often speak of the nafs, the self, as moving between states, with the hope of one day being addressed as the soul at rest; the last verses of Al-Fajr are often recalled in times of loss.

o: nightfall, when the sun has fully set
the dawn, sworn by at the start of Surah 89
the final call to return to the Lord

games.q: what's inside the ending — tap the pairs.
p: the self that pushes to harm

s: Al-Fajr ends with a scene of punishment
its last four verses speak gently to the soul at rest: return, enter My Garden.
the soul at rest is described as both pleased and pleasing
content with its Lord, and its Lord content with it.
the three states of the soul all come from one verse
they're drawn from three surahs: 12:53, 75:2, and here, 89:27.

games.q: after the earth is flattened and people wish they'd done more, Al-Fajr turns to one soul. what does it tell that soul?
games.why: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure (89:27–28). the storm ends in a homecoming.

practice: Don't try to be calm; just stop stirring, and let your shoulders come down the way they do when you get home. If thoughts swirl, let them, the way silt swirls before it sinks.
At the end, notice whether anything settled, even a little.

wordCard.voice: Al-Fajr. The dawn, Surah eighty-nine, which ends by calling the soul at rest to return, pleased and pleasing. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "at rest, settled," from t-m-n, the same root as hearts finding rest in 13:28.

carryVoice: Your line: soul at rest, return. That's all of Al-Fajr, from dawn to homecoming. See you tomorrow.
